splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to an agency's anti-defendant interpretation of ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This matters because it directly affects sentence lengths for defendants whose enhancements depend on ambiguous guideline terms.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to Sentencing Commission commentary takes priority over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous guidelines to control.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary can validly expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy and attempt when the guideline text itself does not mention such offenses. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions qualify for the career-offender enhancement, significantly increasing their sentencing range.

positions.label: Commentary is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, so inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses because it does not mention them, and the commentary impermissibly expands the guideline's scope, so conspiracy convictions do not qualify as controlled substance offenses.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1) of the First Step Act's safety-valve provision is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in the safety-valve provision means defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is disqualifying. This split directly affects mandatory minimum sentences for drug offenders across the country.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive (all three required to disqualify)
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' as conjunctive.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies)
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as disjunctive or distributive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state's drug schedules are broader than the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether USSG § 4B1.2(b)'s definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally controlled or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with prior state drug convictions involving substances not on federal schedules.

positions.label: State schedules suffice
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines includes offenses under state law regardless of whether the specific substance is federally controlled, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that a state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, requiring a categorical match.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's amendments to § 924(c) stacking, can constitute or contribute to 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive statutory changes in sentencing law can serve as a basis for compassionate release. Some circuits hold that such changes can never be considered, while others allow them as a factor. This affects potentially thousands of federal prisoners serving sentences that would be lower under current law.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot contribute
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly when combined with other factors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) rather than civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens) to challenge conditions of confinement, and whether habeas extends to challenges beyond the fact or duration of confinement.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) may be brought as habeas claims, civil rights claims, or both. The Supreme Court left this question open in Preiser v. Rodriguez and has not resolved it, creating confusion among circuits on the proper vehicle for BOP challenges including First Step Act earned-time-credits disputes.

positions.label: Habeas available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus may be used to challenge conditions or terms of confinement, not just the fact or duration of imprisonment, particularly when prisoners seek release-related relief.

positions.label: Habeas limited to fact/duration of confinement
positions.summary: Holds that habeas corpus is limited to challenges to the fact or duration of confinement, and conditions-of-confinement claims must proceed through civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for the underlying violation of supervised release conditions, or whether revocation sentences must be oriented solely toward the goals of supervised release (reintegration, public safety).
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit stands at the extreme of a circuit split by allowing district courts expressly to punish defendants for violations of supervised release, while other circuits hold that supervised release revocation is not about punishment for the violation but about promoting reentry and protecting the public. This affects sentencing for hundreds of supervised release revocations each year.

positions.label: Punishment for the violation is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose sentences at revocation to punish the defendant for the conduct that violated supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must focus on reentry/public safety
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the defendant's breach of trust and reintegration needs, not on punishing the defendant for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for an order on a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees follows the civil timeline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal timeline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the longer civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the shorter criminal deadline). This matters because using the wrong deadline can result in dismissal of the appeal.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 60-day civil appeal deadline applies. This is the majority view.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that the Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in a debtor's assets between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the estate or the debtor. This creates significant uncertainty for debtors who convert in good faith, as their home equity gains may be seized by the trustee depending on the circuit.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means that post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to good-faith converting debtors, not the estate.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing for when actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability must be set. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans, as post-measurement-date assumption changes can significantly alter withdrawal liability calculations.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be established by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), preventing actuaries from selecting assumptions after that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select or update actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, so long as the assumptions are reasonable, because the statute does not impose a deadline on assumption selection.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release and raises questions about judicial power to extend punishment without explicit statutory authorization.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled during absconding, pausing the clock and extending the period during which the court retains jurisdiction to revoke supervised release.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling the term of supervised release during absconding, and judicial creation of such a doctrine exceeds courts' authority.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether the gatekeeping provision of § 2244(b)(1), which categorically bars claims previously presented in habeas, applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter barrier than Congress may have intended, being barred from raising any previously presented claim regardless of new evidence or constitutional rules.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s categorical bar on previously presented claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, and such prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law governing election administration (such as mail-in ballot counting deadlines) before the election takes place.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to state voting procedures. The outcome affects whether election rules can be challenged before votes are cast or only after, with significant implications for mail-in voting, ballot counting, and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate suffers a concrete injury from election rules that allegedly dilute lawful votes or change the electorate, granting standing to challenge such rules pre-election.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's alleged injury from a state election law is too speculative or generalized to confer Article III standing for a pre-election challenge.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost if review were delayed. Other circuits have taken different approaches to the collateral order doctrine's application to sealing orders, creating potential disagreement on when privacy-based sealing denials qualify for immediate appeal.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable because they can be reviewed on appeal from final judgment, and expanding the collateral order doctrine risks piecemeal appeals.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards applicable to discrimination claims arising in hospitality and service industry contexts, including questions about liability and remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently contested.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Adopts broader standards for establishing discrimination liability in hospitality or service establishments, with more expansive remedies available.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, limiting the scope of liability and available damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
